s10-meet~idea.cta: Meet the brief on the Sentence road
s10-meet~idea.title: Meet the brief
s10-meet~idea.body: A brief is a set of rules a sentence must meet, all at once. Check each rule separately against each sentence: Is it one sentence? How does it begin — a subordinate clause has its own subject and verb? Is there a list of three, in matching shapes? Does each semicolon join two complete sentences, or separate list items that already contain commas?
s10-meet~idea.more: I can choose the sentence that meets every rule of a brief.

s10-meet~story.cta: Meet the brief on the Sentence road
s10-meet~story.title: Meet the brief
s10-meet~story.body: Quill has a job card: "One sentence. Start with a when-clause. Include three things." Quill grins. "A writer can build any sentence to order — if every rule is checked, one at a time."
s10-meet~story.more: Taught at: Sentence 10 · Sentences on demand — Meet the brief.

s10-meet~eg.cta: Meet the brief on the Sentence road
s10-meet~eg.title: Meet the brief: for example
s10-meet~eg.body: Brief: begins with a subordinate clause; contains a list of three. · When the storm passed, we found branches, leaves and a broken kite.
s10-meet~eg.more: Taught at: Sentence 10 · Sentences on demand — Meet the brief.

s10-meet~q0.title: Meet the brief

play.q: Which sentence meets ALL of these rules: it begins with a subordinate clause; it contains a list of three?
opts: When the storm passed, we found branches, leaves and a broken kite.
After the storm, we found branches, leaves and a broken kite.
When the storm passed, we found branches and a broken kite.
We found branches, leaves and a broken kite when the storm passed.

s10-meet~q1.cta: Meet the brief on the Sentence road
s10-meet~q1.title: Meet the brief

play.q: Which sentence meets ALL of these rules: it is one sentence; it uses a semicolon correctly?
opts: The fox was hungry; the henhouse was locked.
The fox was hungry; because the henhouse was locked.
The fox was hungry. The henhouse was locked tight.
The fox was hungry, and the henhouse was locked.

play.q: Which sentence meets ALL of these rules: it begins with an -ing phrase; it uses a semicolon correctly?

Hearing the whistle, Bobbie ran to the fence, for the train was coming.
When she heard the whistle, Bobbie ran to the fence; the train was coming.
Hearing the whistle; Bobbie ran to the fence.

play.q: Which sentence meets ALL of these rules: it is one sentence; it begins with a subordinate clause; it uses a semicolon correctly?

opts: After three days of searching the hills, the shepherd found his lamb.
The shepherd found his lamb after three days of searching the hills.

s10-meet~q7.title: Meet the brief

We visited Pune, in India, Paris, in France, and also Lima, in Peru.

s10-meet~q11.cta: Meet the brief on the Sentence road
s10-meet~q11.title: Meet the brief

play.q: Which sentence meets ALL of these rules: it is one sentence; it begins with a subordinate clause; it contains a list of three; it uses a semicolon correctly?
opts: When winter came, the birds left, the pond froze and the fields turned white; only the robin stayed.
When winter came, the birds left, the pond froze and the fields turned white. Only the robin stayed behind.
When winter came, the birds left and the pond froze; only the robin stayed.
The birds left, the pond froze and the fields turned white when winter came; only the robin stayed.

s10-check~idea.cta: Check against the brief on the Sentence road
s10-check~idea.title: Check against the brief
s10-check~idea.body: Checking your own sentence against a brief is the same skill as building one. Go rule by rule: count the sentences (full stops), look at the first words (a subordinate clause has a joining word like when, because or although, then a subject and a verb), count the list, and test each semicolon — could the words on each side stand alone?
s10-check~idea.more: I can find the rule a sentence misses.

s10-check~story.cta: Check against the brief on the Sentence road
s10-check~story.title: Check against the brief
s10-check~story.body: Quill is the editor today, with a red pencil and a brief pinned to the desk. "Each of these sentences nearly made it," says Quill. "Find the one rule each one missed."
s10-check~story.more: Taught at: Sentence 10 · Sentences on demand — Check against the brief.

wr10-model~idea.title: In the manner of…
wr10-model~idea.body: Read a model, notice what makes it special — its opening, its voice, its repeated phrases — then write your own piece that borrows those things. This is how writers have always learned.

sp10-debate~idea.title: Both sides
sp10-debate~idea.body: First argue FOR the motion: your three best reasons. Then argue AGAINST it, just as fairly. Arguing the side you disagree with is how you learn to understand people who disagree with you.
sp10-debate~idea.more: I can argue for a motion, then against it, fairly and clearly.

li10-case~idea.where: Literature 10 · My case for this book
li10-case~idea.cta: My case for this book at the writing desk
li10-case~idea.title: My case for this book
li10-case~idea.body: A case has a claim, reasons, evidence from the book itself — a line, a moment — an answer to the other side, and a close. You are not marked on which book you choose, only on how well you argue for it.
li10-case~idea.more: I can make the case for a book I love, with reasons and lines from it.
